summary: Describes an operational practice for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) that makes domain transfers between registrars more secure. Instead of long-lived passwords, it uses strong random authorization values that are short lived and not stored in plain form by the registrar. It relies on the existing EPP specifications rather than changing them.

eli5.summary: To move a domain, you need a secret code. This says the code should be random, used briefly, and then thrown away.

questions: how to securely transfer a domain with epp
how do secure domain transfers work
how long should an epp auth code be
subtitle: A way to move a domain between registrars using short-lived, random, hashed transfer codes instead of long-lived passwords.

tldr.problem: EPP transfer authorization info is usually a long-lived password set when an object is created and stored in a form the registry can decrypt, which is a latent risk of compromise.
tldr.mechanism: The losing registrar generates a strong random value only when a transfer starts, the registry stores just a salted hash of it, and the value is cleared when the transfer completes or its TTL expires.
tldr.outcome: It needs no new protocol, only existing EPP features that client and server signal with a namespace URI. It is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Hash size
facts.value: At least 256 bits, such as SHA-256

today: RFC 9154 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and IANA registered it in the EPP extension registry with status Active.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP, RFC 5730) uses authorization information to authorize a transfer of an object, such as a domain name, between registrars. In the domain and contact mappings (RFC 5731, RFC 5733) this is a password. In practice it is set at creation, managed with updates and used to authorize transfers.

The RFC says the original lifecycle involves long-term storage of encrypted (not hashed) passwords. That is a significant latent risk of compromise and does not match current best practice. RFC 9154 defines an operational practice, using the existing EPP RFCs, with three elements: strong random values, short lifetimes, and secure storage. It is not a new protocol. The domain name object is used for illustration, but the practice applies to any EPP object.
sections.eli5: Today the secret code for moving a domain often sits around for years. This says to make a fresh, hard-to-guess code only when you need it.

sections.title: Registrant, Registrar and Registry
sections.content:
EPP names only a client and a server, but a transfer involves three actors, defined using RFC 8499.

  • The registrant owns the object and coordinates the transfer.
  • The registrar is the go-between and is the EPP client. The sponsoring registrar is authorized to manage the object. In a transfer, the losing registrar gives up the object and the gaining registrar receives it. A registrar may reach the registrant through resellers, and the practice extends through that channel.
  • The registry operates the zone and is the EPP server. It records the sponsoring registrar for each object.

The authorization information is meant to authenticate the registrant as the owner to the non-sponsoring registrar and authorize the transfer.
sections.eli5: You own a toy, one shop looks after it, and a big office keeps the records. Moving it to a new shop needs a code only you were given.

sections.title: Signaling Support
sections.content:
Client and server signal support with the namespace URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:epp:secure-authinfo-transfer-1.0. The client puts it in an <extURI> element of the <login> command. The server puts it in the greeting.

A client that sees the URI in the greeting can expect the server to support:

  • an empty authorization value on <create>;
  • unsetting it with <update>;
  • validating it with <info>;
  • not telling a non-sponsoring registrar whether it is set;
  • returning an empty value to the sponsoring registrar when it is set;
  • accepting a matching non-empty value to authorize a transfer;
  • automatically unsetting it after a successful transfer.

A server that sees the URI in the login can expect the client to generate secure random values and to set the value only while a transfer is in process.
sections.eli5: Both sides hold up a card saying "I know the new rules" before they start using them.

sections.title: What Makes Authorization Information Secure
sections.content:
Random. The value MUST be generated from a secure random source. Implementations SHOULD use at least 128 bits of entropy. The RFC computes the length from the character set: 20 characters from the 94 printable ASCII characters other than space, or 25 characters from a 36-character alphanumeric set.

Short lived. The value SHOULD be set only while a transfer is in process, so it has a TTL after which it is cleared. The sponsoring registrar chooses the TTL and MUST tell the registrant what it is.

Stored safely. The registry MUST store it with a strong one-way hash of at least 256 bits, such as SHA-256, and a per-value random salt of at least 128 bits. The losing registrar MUST NOT store it, and the gaining registrar may keep it only as a transient value. Plain text MUST NOT be logged. It MUST travel over encrypted channels, including the registrar's interface to the registrant.

Matching. An unset value is stored as NULL. Any input value MUST NOT match an unset value, an empty input MUST NOT match any set value, and a non-empty input is hashed and compared with the stored hash.
sections.eli5: The code is long and random, lives only a short time, and the office keeps only a scrambled copy that cannot be turned back into the code.

sections.title: The Transfer Flow and EPP Commands
sections.content:
The steps are as follows. The registrar sends <create> with an empty value. When a transfer is wanted, the losing registrar generates a random value, sets it with <update> and gives it to the registrant. The registrant passes it to the gaining registrar, which may check it with <info> and then sends the <transfer> request. On success the registry automatically unsets it. Otherwise the losing registrar unsets it when the TTL expires.

Per command:

  • Create: the registry MUST accept an empty value and MAY refuse a non-empty one.
  • Update: the registry MUST allow setting and unsetting. Registrars often need to remove clientTransferProhibited first. A registry may check strength heuristically and return error 2202, so registrars must be ready to generate a new value and retry. When the TTL expires the registrar MUST unset the value.
  • Info: a non-empty value is checked against the hash. If it is unset or does not match, the registry MUST return 2202. The response MUST NOT include a non-empty value, and the registry MUST NOT reveal to a non-sponsoring registrar whether the value is set.
  • Transfer request: a non-empty value is hashed and compared. On a mismatch or unset value the registry MUST return 2202. A transfer returns 1000 if immediate or 1001 if pending, and the losing registrar MUST be told through a <poll> message.
sections.eli5: When you want to move, your shop makes a fresh secret code and gives it to you. You hand it to the new shop, the office checks it, and then the code is wiped.

sections.title: Transition From the Classic Model
sections.content:
The RFC treats the "Classic Authorization Information Model" as the starting point: a non-empty value at creation, kept for the life of the object, stored encrypted and retrievable through <info>. It suggests three phases for a registry.

  • Phase 1, Features: allow an empty value on create, allow unsetting on update, automatically unset on transfer approval, stop returning the value in info responses, and return 2202 for both unset and non-matching values. The info change is the only one that is not optional for registrars and could break clients, so notice is recommended.
  • Phase 2, Storage: hash new values, compare against either hashed or encrypted values, and convert existing encrypted values to hashes, invisibly to registrars.
  • Phase 3, Enforcement: disallow a non-empty value on create, which may break clients, and validate at least 128 bits of entropy on update.
sections.eli5: Switching from the old way to the new way happens in steps, so nobody gets locked out in the middle.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section restates the core requirements: at least 128 bits of entropy, a transfer-only lifetime with the registrant told the TTL, and hashed storage with a salt. The losing registrar stores nothing, the gaining registrar keeps only a transient copy, plain text is never logged, and the value travels only over encrypted channels. Storing unset values as NULL ensures an empty input never matches.

The RFC also says secure transfers matter to mitigate theft, fraud and other abuse, so it is critical that registrars use only strong, randomly generated values.
sections.eli5: Make the code hard to guess, keep it briefly, never write it on a sticky note, and only whisper it over a private line.
